questions.title: How does the D.C. Circuit distinguish between a 'standalone' declaration and an 'update' when determining if Exemption 7(A) pendency requirements are met?
questions.question_body: The court affirms the FBI's use of a brief 'Bender declaration' to confirm that an investigation remains ongoing, despite Farahi arguing it was conclusory. The court accepts this because it views the Bender declaration as merely updating the earlier, detailed 'Hardy declarations.' I am confused about the evidentiary threshold here: Does this mean that once an agency establishes pendency with a robust affidavit, subsequent updates can be significantly thinner? How far can an agency push this logic before a plaintiff can successfully argue that the agency has failed to meet its burden of proof regarding current pendency?

questions.title: What is the practical application of 'inextricably intertwined' vs. 'random interspersion' in FOIA segregability analysis for large volumes of data?
questions.question_body: Section V discusses segregability. The court rejects Farahi's argument that there must be some releasable info just because there are thousands of pages, citing *Mead*. They state that if non-exempt material is 'interspersed line-by-line,' it isn't reasonably segregable. But my confusion lies in the definition of 'meaningful information.' If I have 10,000 pages where 99% is redacted under 7(A), and the remaining 1% consists of isolated names or dates scattered throughout, why is extracting those specific fragments legally impossible or unreasonable? Is the test purely about whether the extracted text conveys independent meaning without revealing the exempt context?

questions.title: Can a defendant effectively waive their right to challenge ex parte/sealed submissions by failing to explicitly oppose their admission into the record?
questions.question_body: In paragraph V, the court notes that Farahi cannot complain about the district court relying heavily on Bender's ex parte declaration for segregability analysis because 'Farahi did not oppose the district court’s acceptance of ex parte declarations.' This seems like a major procedural trap. If I am representing a FOIA requester and I suspect my opponent will submit sensitive classified info via ex parte affidavit, do I need to file a specific motion objecting to *any* potential reliance on sealed materials, even if I don't know exactly what they contain yet? Or does silence equal waiver for all future challenges regarding those specific sealed submissions?

questions.title: Does conceding involvement in terrorist activities during parallel immigration proceedings automatically satisfy the 'law enforcement purpose' nexus requirement for FOIA Exemption 7(A)?
questions.question_body: In Section IV-A, the court relies partly on Farahi's own concession from his immigration case (where he admitted being linked to terrorists) to find that his FBI file was compiled for law enforcement purposes. Usually, courts require a specific nexus between the document creation and law enforcement duties. Here, it seems like admitting guilt/liability in another forum helped satisfy this element here. Does this create a precedent where a party's admissions in administrative or civil litigation can shortcut the government's burden to prove the original intent behind compiling records under Exemption 7?

questions.title: Is there a difference between 'pending' and 'reasonably anticipated' proceedings when dealing with ongoing criminal investigations versus civil immigration hearings?
questions.question_body: The opinion mentions that 'ongoing criminal investigations count as proceedings' under 7(A). However, Farahi's background involves both criminal investigations and immigration (civil) removal proceedings. The court cites *Juarez* regarding gathering evidence for a 'possible future criminal case.' My confusion is whether Exemption 7(A) treats an active internal FBI intelligence gathering phase differently than a formal indictment or an open immigration hearing. Specifically, does the threat of interference apply equally if no charges have been filed yet but only an internal intelligence investigation is underway?

questions.title: How strictly must an agency define document categories when withholding files on a categorical basis, especially when national security is involved?
questions.question_body: In Section IV-C, Farahi argued that the FBI didn't define its document categories sufficiently distinctively to allow judicial review. The court dismissed this because Farahi offered no specific explanation of *why* they were overbroad ('forfeited his arguments'). This raises two questions: First, does this imply that if a plaintiff doesn't know enough about the content to critique categories (because they haven't seen them), they are stuck? Second, does deference increase so much in national security cases that generic categories (like 'investigative reports') are sufficient unless challenged with specific examples?
